title: Fatigue life improvement of fillet welded joints by friction stir processing
abstract: Abstract Friction Stir Processing (FSP) is an advanced solid-state surface treatment technique that achieves significant microstructural refinement through frictional heat generation and intense plastic deformation. This study proposes a novel methodology to enhance the fatigue performance of fillet-welded T-joints made of SM490A steel, employing Tilted Friction Stir Processing (TFSP). A total of thirteen fillet-welded specimens, fabricated using SM490A steel base metal and Z3313 T49J0T1-1CA-U weld metal, were examined, with six of them treated by TFSP. A tungsten carbide (WC) tool tilted at an angle of 9° was utilized, rotating at 600 rpm and advancing at a speed of 150 mm/min along the weld toes. Detailed microstructural analyses revealed substantial grain refinement and a 54.8% increase in Vickers hardness within the stir zone (SZ) compared to untreated regions. Four-point bending fatigue tests at a stress ratio  R  = 0.1 were performed, complemented by finite element method (FEM) analysis to elucidate stress distributions and crack initiation behaviors. Results demonstrated that TFSP significantly prolongs fatigue life, primarily due to a synergistic combination of microstructural refinement, hardness enhancement, and mitigation of stress concentration at the weld toe. Although TFSP introduced localized changes in residual stress, these had negligible adverse effects on fatigue performance. The findings underscore the efficacy of TFSP as a practical technique for fatigue improvement in welded steel structures.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Steel structures, particularly steel bridges, are widely adopted due to their outstanding mechanical properties, including high strength, excellent ductility, and adaptability. Their ease of fabrication enables flexible designs suitable for various structural configurations, while their prefabrication potential considerably enhances on-site assembly efficiency. Among steel bridge components, welded joints play a pivotal role in connecting structural members, critically influencing the bridge’s structural integrity and long-term reliability [ 1 ,  2 ]. However, fillet-welded T-joints, frequently used in frame structures, are especially susceptible to fatigue cracking under cyclic loading conditions. Fatigue cracks typically initiate at weld toes, known sites of high stress concentration, subsequently propagating and potentially leading to premature structural failures [ 3 ,  4 ]. Although extensive studies have focused on mitigating fatigue problems at weld toes, the persistence of fatigue-related failures highlights the urgent need for more effective treatment methods.

Several conventional post-weld treatments, including weld grinding, ultrasonic peening, hammer peening, and shot peening, have been extensively investigated for their fatigue improvement capabilities [ 5 ,  6 ,  7 ,  8 ,  9 – 10 ]. Weld grinding primarily reduces stress concentrations by improving weld toe geometry, effectively increasing fatigue life. However, its beneficial effects significantly diminish under high fatigue stress amplitudes, making it less reliable for critical structural components [ 6 ,  7 ]. Ultrasonic peening, on the other hand, modifies residual stress distribution and introduces beneficial compressive residual stresses at weld toes, thus enhancing fatigue resistance. Nevertheless, its effectiveness heavily depends on stringent control of process parameters, potentially limiting practical implementation due to complexity and associated quality control challenges [ 8 ,  9 – 10 ]. These traditional approaches have thus encountered inherent trade-offs between the quality of fatigue improvement and process simplicity, underscoring the necessity for alternative solutions that combine robust fatigue enhancement with process feasibility and repeatability.

Recently, Friction Stir Processing (FSP), a solid-state surface modification technique derived from friction stir welding (FSW), has emerged as a promising approach for enhancing material fatigue properties. Originally developed by The Welding Institute (TWI) in 1991, FSW revolutionized welding technologies by enabling high-strength, defect-free joints without melting the base material [ 11 ,  12 – 13 ]. The fundamental mechanism involves a rotating, non-consumable tool that generates frictional heat and intense plastic deformation, producing a refined, dynamically recrystallized microstructure with significantly improved mechanical properties [ 14 ,  15 – 16 ]. This solid-state characteristic is shared by linear friction welding (LFW), which joins materials through frictional heating and intense plastic deformation without bulk melting. In contrast to fusion welding, solid-state techniques suppress solidification-related defects such as porosity, segregation, and hot cracking, while limiting the extent of the heat-affected zone and reducing thermal distortion. The combination of severe plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization produces refined and homogeneous microstructures with improved metallurgical continuity. Studies on LFW of titanium alloys and superalloys have demonstrated that properly controlled solid-state joints can achieve mechanical properties comparable to or exceeding those of the base material, owing to grain refinement and the absence of detrimental solidification structures [ 17 ,  18 ]. Building on the fundamental principles of FSW, FSP was developed as a localized surface treatment method for enhancing the mechanical properties of specific structural areas without joining components. Studies have reported notable fatigue performance enhancements in various metallic alloys through microstructural refinement achieved via FSP [ 19 ,  20 ]. For example, Costa et al. [ 19 ] demonstrated substantial fatigue life improvements of aluminum MIG-welded T-joints by applying FSP, attributed to effective grain refinement and residual stress redistribution. Yamamoto et al. [ 20 ] similarly reported significant fatigue life extension in steel butt-welded joints after applying spherical-tip tungsten carbide tools for localized surface modification using FSP, primarily due to improved weld geometry and microstructural refinement near weld toes. Despite these advancements, the application of FSP to enhance fatigue resistance specifically in fillet-welded T-joints of steel structures remains largely unexplored. Compared to butt-welded joints, fillet welds present more complex geometrical and stress-concentration conditions, thus requiring tailored FSP strategies to effectively reduce local stress concentrations and inhibit fatigue crack initiation. Tilted Friction Stir Processing (TFSP), involving a strategically inclined tool relative to the surface normal, has recently been proposed as an effective approach for improving surface geometry and controlling flash formation, hence potentially offering substantial fatigue performance improvements [ 21 ,  22 ,  23 – 24 ]. However, the effectiveness of TFSP in enhancing fatigue life of steel fillet-welded T-joints has yet to be systematically investigated, leaving a critical research gap in understanding its applicability and mechanisms.

In this context, the present study aims to systematically evaluate the fatigue enhancement potential of TFSP applied to fillet-welded T-joints fabricated from SM490A steel. Specifically, the study investigates the effects of TFSP parameters—such as tool inclination angle, rotation speed, and travel speed—on microstructural evolution, surface geometry optimization, hardness distribution, and residual stress modification. Comprehensive four-point bending fatigue tests coupled with detailed finite element method (FEM) analyses were conducted to elucidate the relationship between local stress conditions, fatigue crack initiation behavior, and resulting fatigue life improvements. The results of this investigation not only fill a critical knowledge gap regarding TFSP’s fatigue enhancement capabilities but also provide practical insights into the potential application of TFSP as a reliable fatigue countermeasure for welded steel infrastructure.

sections.heading: Materials and specimen preparation
paragraphs:
The materials used in this investigation comprised SM490A structural steel as the base material and JIS Z3313 T49J0T1-1CA-U as the filler metal, both of which are commonly utilized in steel bridge constructions. The chemical compositions and mechanical properties of the base and filler materials are summarized in Table  1 . The SM490A steel exhibits good weldability and mechanical strength, making it suitable for structural engineering applications subject to cyclic loading conditions, such as bridges and frame structures.

The T-joint specimens used in this study consisted of a skin plate measuring 300 mm in length, 200 mm in width, and 12 mm in thickness, joined to a longitudinal rib plate measuring 12 mm in height, 200 mm in length, and 12 mm in thickness as shown in Fig.  1 . Prior to welding, surface contaminants such as rust, grease, and mill scale were thoroughly removed by mechanical grinding and subsequent cleaning with acetone. To minimize the initial residual stresses inherent in steel fabrication, the plates were first temporarily tack-welded at the corners using spot welding and subsequently annealed at 600 °C for 2 h, followed by air cooling to room temperature. Fig. 1 Dimensions of specimens

Semi-automatic CO₂ gas-shielded arc welding (GMAW) was employed to fabricate the fillet-welded T-joints. During welding, the plates were firmly clamped onto a rigid welding table equipped with custom-designed clamps to prevent deformation and ensure consistent weld quality. The welding conditions adopted in this investigation, including voltage, current, and welding speed, are summarized in Table  2 . These welding parameters were selected based on preliminary welding trials, with the goal of achieving adequate weld penetration, uniform weld bead profiles, and sufficient structural integrity typical for practical steel bridge components. Subsequently, the welded plates were cut to obtain test specimens, each 140 mm wide, by removing 30 mm from both ends of the weld bead to eliminate potential irregularities associated with weld initiation and termination regions.

Among the thirteen prepared specimens, six were designated for tilted TFSP treatment, while the remaining seven served as the control group under as-welded (AW) conditions. Prior to TFSP treatment, specimens were carefully cleaned again to remove surface oxides and contaminants, ensuring optimal conditions for subsequent surface processing.

sections.heading: Tilted Friction Stir Processing (TFSP) method
paragraphs: The TFSP employed in this study utilized a custom-designed tungsten carbide (WC) tool, carefully selected due to its high hardness, exceptional wear resistance, and suitability for processing high-strength structural steels. The tool featured a cylindrical shoulder with a diameter of 15 mm and a probe length of 7.5 mm, optimized based on preliminary trials to achieve effective stirring depth and sufficient heat generation for the SM490A steel plates employed.

To maximize the efficacy of microstructural refinement at the weld toe, the tool was strategically tilted at an angle of 9° relative to the specimen’s vertical axis. The selection of a 9° tilt angle was based on prior research and preliminary testing, demonstrating improved surface finishing, controlled burr formation, and optimized material flow near the weld toes. During processing, the tool rotated at a constant speed of 600 rpm while progressing along the weld toe at a travel speed of 150 mm/min, parameters that were systematically determined from preliminary parametric studies aimed at balancing heat input, tool wear, and effective microstructural refinement. The final parameter combination was down-selected from preliminary trials based on defined screening criteria. These criteria included minimal flash or burr formation at the weld toe, improved surface smoothness and increased toe radius, sufficient stir zone coverage of the fatigue-critical region without surface defects (e.g., grooves, undercut, or insufficient stirring), noticeable hardness enhancement compared to the as-welded condition, and stable processing behavior without excessive tool vibration or abnormal loading. The selected parameters satisfied all these requirements and ensured repeatable and defect-free processing. Each specimen was securely fixed using specially designed rigid steel fixtures, clamping both sides of the plates firmly onto a heavy-duty worktable. The robust fixture system was essential for mitigating out-of-plane deformation during TFSP and ensuring a consistent processing depth and tool trajectory. To precisely control the depth of the stir SZ, the tool shoulder was positioned to reach approximately 3.2 mm below the specimen’s top surface, allowing sufficient penetration to refine microstructure effectively at critical stress-concentration zones without thinning the surface material.

In conventional FSP of butt-welded joints, positioning the retreating side (RS) of the tool at the weld toe has proven beneficial due to the natural deposition of plasticized material, filling weld toe imperfections [ 20 ]. However, preliminary tests indicated that for fillet-welded T-joints—characterized by more complex geometries—such configurations led to problematic flash (or burr) accumulation and increased local stress concentration. Hence, the advancing side (AS) of the tool, where more intensive plastic deformation and stirring occurs due to the tool’s forward motion, was intentionally positioned adjacent to the weld toe. This strategic choice effectively minimized flash formation at the weld toe, ensuring smoother surface geometry and reduced stress concentrations. During processing, each side of the weld bead was treated separately. After completing TFSP on one side, the specimen was allowed to cool naturally to room temperature before processing the opposite side. This interval of controlled cooling between the two-sided processing minimized thermal distortion and residual stress gradients, resulting in more uniform microstructural refinement and balanced residual stress distributions across the weld region.

Figure  2 (a) provides a schematic illustration clearly showing the TFSP tool geometry, including the dimensions and tilt angle (9°), as well as the tool’s rotational direction, traveling direction, and relative positions of AS and RS. Figure  2 (b) presents an actual photograph taken during TFSP processing, demonstrating the practical implementation of the setup, including the tool position and fixture system. Fig. 2 Schematic diagrams of FSP: ( a ) setting and parameters of FSP; ( b ) on-site processing work

The selected TFSP parameters, including tilt angle, rotation speed, and travel speed, along with the strategic placement of AS near the weld toe, were comprehensively analyzed in subsequent sections to elucidate their individual and combined contributions to fatigue performance enhancement, microstructural refinement, hardness improvement, and residual stress redistribution.

sections.heading: Surface geometry and microstructural characterization
paragraphs: The surface geometry near the weld toes was quantitatively evaluated to investigate the effects of TFSP on local stress concentration factors. A laser displacement sensor system (KEYENCE, LK-G5000V; accuracy ± 0.05 mm) was utilized for high-precision measurements. Each specimen was positioned horizontally on a precision translation stage, and the laser sensor scanned across the joint region perpendicular to the weld direction at a controlled speed of 30 mm/s, with measurement intervals of 0.1 mm to capture micro-geometrical features such as burrs, flash, and surface irregularities. Key geometric parameters, particularly the weld toe radius, were extracted from the recorded profile data and compared between TFSP-treated and as-welded (AW) specimens to evaluate the effectiveness of TFSP in reducing stress concentrations.

For microstructural characterization, cross-sectional samples were extracted from both TFSP-treated and AW specimens. Specimens were cut perpendicular to the weld line, embedded in epoxy resin, ground with silicon carbide papers, polished with diamond suspensions, and etched with 2% nital solution to reveal microstructural features. Optical microscopy (100 × –400 ×) was then performed to examine distinct zones, including the weld metal (WM), heat-affected zone (HAZ), base metal (BM), stir zone (SZ), and the SZ-HAZ transition region (SZ/HAZ interface), with particular focus on grain refinement, phase distribution, and the microstructural transition across the processed boundary. These observations provided essential insights into the microstructural mechanisms contributing to the observed enhancements in hardness and fatigue resistance following TFSP treatment.

sections.heading: Vickers hardness measurement
paragraphs: To quantitatively evaluate the effects of TFSP-induced microstructural refinement on local mechanical properties around the weld toes, Vickers hardness measurements were systematically conducted on cross-sectional specimens prepared previously for microstructural characterization, ensuring consistency between microstructural observations and mechanical evaluations. A micro-Vickers hardness tester (MICROHARDNESS TESTER FM series) was employed for measurements along horizontal lines positioned precisely at a depth of 1 mm beneath the top surface, chosen to capture hardness values from regions significantly affected by TFSP while avoiding surface roughness influences.

Vickers hardness tests were carried out under a constant load of 0.98 N (100 gf) with a dwell time of 15 s per indentation, complying with ASTM E384 standard guidelines. Indentations were spaced at 0.2 mm intervals along the measurement line, covering the region of interest from BM through HAZ, WM, SZ-HAZ transition region, and finally the SZ. Each indentation was examined microscopically to verify the absence of visible cracks or irregularities. Multiple indentation lines were performed for each specimen type (AW and TFSP-treated), and hardness values were statistically averaged at each corresponding position. The resulting hardness distributions were plotted against spatial positions to illustrate and quantify the effects of TFSP on local mechanical properties.

sections.heading: Residual stress measurement
paragraphs: To evaluate the effects of TFSP on residual stress distributions near weld toes, measurements were performed using a portable X-ray diffraction (XRD)-based residual stress analyzer (μ-X360s, Pulstec Industrial Co., Ltd.). The analyzer operates based on the cosα method, irradiating the specimen surface with a collimated Cr-Kα X-ray beam at an incident angle of approximately 35°. Residual stresses were determined by analyzing shifts in diffraction peak positions obtained from a high-sensitivity two-dimensional detector.

Measurements were systematically conducted on both as-welded (AW) and TFSP-treated specimens along transverse lines at 5 mm intervals, covering regions from 15 to 40 mm away from the weld centerline on each side. At each location, both transverse and longitudinal residual stresses were independently recorded. Prior to measurements, specimen surfaces were cleaned and gently polished to minimize surface roughness effects. Reference stress-free samples were used for calibration. Mean values and standard deviations were calculated for each measurement point, and the resulting stress distributions were analyzed to identify TFSP-induced alterations relative to the AW condition.

sections.heading: Fatigue experiment procedure
paragraphs: To evaluate the effectiveness of TFSP in enhancing the fatigue life of fillet-welded T-joints, four-point bending fatigue experiments were systematically conducted on both TFSP-treated and as-welded (AW) specimens. The four-point bending configuration was selected because it provides a constant bending moment region along the weld line, where fatigue cracks typically initiate. Each specimen had a width of 140 mm and was extracted from the original welded plates to ensure geometric consistency. To monitor local deformation and detect crack onset, strain gauges (5 mm gauge length) were attached near the weld toes on the tension side, with positions determined based on preliminary finite element analysis.

Fatigue experiments were performed on a servo-hydraulic testing machine under load control using a constant-amplitude sinusoidal waveform with a stress ratio of  R  = 0.1 and a frequency of 5 Hz. The applied load ranges were selected to generate nominal stress ranges of 210, 225, 240, 255, and 270 MPa, covering both high-cycle and medium-cycle fatigue regimes relevant to structural applications. The nominal stress was calculated from the applied load using the classical beam bending relationship for four-point bending, assuming linear elastic behavior. The load-stress conversion was further verified through finite element analysis to ensure consistency between analytical estimation and local stress distribution along the weld line. The corresponding applied load ranges are summarized in Table  3  together with the fatigue experiment conditions for completeness.

Specimens were supported in a symmetrical four-point bending configuration with inner and outer spans of 100 mm and 240 mm, respectively (Fig.  3 ). Tests continued until failure or until reaching a predefined endurance limit of 2,592,000 cycles. Failure was defined by either fatigue crack detection via periodic magnetic particle inspection or a reduction in strain gauge signal amplitude of at least 5% from its stabilized cyclic value. Post-test visual and magnetic particle inspections were conducted to confirm crack initiation locations and propagation paths.
Fig. 3 Schematic diagrams of the fatigue experiment: ( a ) setup of fatigue load; ( b ) experiment situation; ( c ) strain gauge locations

sections.heading: Finite Element Method (FEM) analysis
paragraphs: Finite Element Method (FEM) analysis was employed to investigate and quantify local stress concentrations at the weld toes of both TFSP-treated and as-welded (AW) specimens under four-point bending fatigue loading conditions. The experimentally identified fatigue crack initiation sites in Fig.  4 , marked by blue circles, were used to define the critical regions for stress concentration evaluation. The FEM analysis was performed on the cross-sections indicated by the red lines, providing detailed insights into stress distributions and the locations of maximum local stress, which were then compared with the experimentally observed crack initiation positions. Simple two-dimensional, plane-strain elastic finite element models were constructed using the ABAQUS software (version 6.18). Model geometries accurately reflected the actual dimensions and measured weld toe geometries of experimental specimens. Material properties were assumed linear-elastic with an elastic modulus of 2.1 × 10 5  N/mm 2  and Poisson’s ratio of 0.3, consistent with typical structural steel characteristics under low-level cyclic stresses. Boundary conditions replicated the experimental four-point bending loading configuration. Refined meshes were employed at weld toe regions to accurately capture stress gradients, while coarser meshes were used elsewhere to optimize computational efficiency. Fig. 4 Fracture surfaces of representative specimens after four-point bending fatigue failure. ( a ) Stress range of 255 N/mm 2 ; ( b ) stress range of 240N/mm 2 ; ( c ) stress range of 270N/mm. 2

The resulting stress concentration factors were systematically compared between TFSP-treated and AW specimens, allowing quantitative evaluation of the geometric and microstructural improvement effects introduced by TFSP. FEM results were validated by comparing stress concentration locations and magnitudes with experimentally observed fatigue crack initiation positions identified through magnetic particle inspections and visual observations.

sections.heading: Effect of TFSP on surface geometry at weld toes
paragraphs: The surface geometry at the weld toes critically influences local stress concentrations, directly affecting fatigue performance. Figure  5  illustrates representative surface profiles measured across weld toes of the as-welded (AW) and TFSP-treated specimens, clearly highlighting the geometric modifications introduced by TFSP. Fig. 5 Specimen size and measurement results of welded joint surface geometry: ( a ) location of the cross-section (red dotted line); ( b ) results of AW and FSP-treated specimens

In the AW condition, the weld toe exhibited notable geometric irregularities characterized by sharp transitions and localized depressions resulting from typical fillet-welding practices. Such geometric irregularities inherently increase local stress concentrations, creating preferential initiation sites for fatigue cracking under cyclic loading conditions. After applying TFSP, substantial improvements in surface geometry were observed. As depicted in Fig.  5 (b), the TFSP-treated region displayed a notably smoother and more regular surface profile adjacent to the weld toe. The strategic placement of the AS of the rotating tool near the weld toe successfully minimized flash formation and burr accumulation, thus significantly reducing geometric discontinuities and surface roughness. Specifically, the weld toe radius was noticeably enlarged, and previously sharp transitions were effectively smoothed, directly contributing to stress concentration reductions. In contrast, a notable flash formation was observed on the RS, away from the weld toe region. This localized flash (highlighted by green circles in Fig.  5 (b)) arose due to material flow characteristics associated with the tool’s rotation direction and inclination angle. However, since this flash was located far from the critical weld toe regions, its impact on local fatigue resistance was considered minimal.

These observed geometric modifications at weld toes after TFSP directly correlate with subsequent reductions in local stress concentration factors, as quantitatively confirmed by FEM analyses presented in later sections (see Sect. 3.4). Consequently, the optimized weld toe geometry achieved through TFSP provides an essential foundation for improved fatigue performance in fillet-welded steel joints.

sections.heading: Microstructural evolution and hardness improvement
paragraphs: The microstructural evolution induced by TFSP treatment significantly influenced local mechanical properties at the weld toe region. Representative optical micrographs obtained from different regions across the specimen cross-section, including the weld metal (WM), heat-affected zone (HAZ), base metal (BM), stir zone (SZ), and the SZ-HAZ transition region, are illustrated clearly in Fig.  6 . In the weld metal (WM) region (Fig.  6 (b)), a characteristic mixed microstructure consisting of bainite and ferrite was observed, featuring coarse and elongated grain morphologies typically generated by arc welding thermal cycles. The adjacent HAZ (Fig.  6 (c)) displayed a predominantly ferritic microstructure with partial bainitic transformation, indicating moderate thermal influence during welding. In contrast, the base metal (BM, Fig.  6 (d)) exhibited a uniform and equiaxed ferritic grain structure, reflecting the original hot-rolled condition of the SM490A steel plate. Notably, in the TFSP-treated region (SZ, Fig.  6 (e)), significant grain refinement was achieved due to intense plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization. The SZ exhibited substantially finer, equiaxed ferritic grains compared to other regions. Furthermore, the SZ-HAZ transition region (Fig.  6 (f)) exhibited partially deformed and partially recrystallized microstructures, reflecting the steep gradients of strain and temperature between the heavily stirred SZ and the purely heat-affected region. From a mechanistic perspective, the WM microstructure (Fig.  6 (b)) is governed by melting/solidification during GMAW and subsequent solid-state transformations upon cooling, which typically produce relatively coarse, heterogeneous ferrite/bainite morphologies. The HAZ (Fig.  6 (c)) does not melt, but experiences a welding thermal cycle; depending on the peak temperature and cooling rate, partial or full austenitization followed by transformation during cooling results in a mixed and spatially heterogeneous microstructure compared with the BM (Fig.  6 (d)). In contrast, the SZ (Fig.  6 (e)) undergoes intense plastic shear deformation under frictional heating during TFSP, promoting dynamic recrystallization and producing fine, equiaxed grains. Across the SZ-HAZ transition region (Fig.  6 (f)), the imposed strain and temperature decrease rapidly with distance from the tool, so recrystallization becomes incomplete and a gradient microstructure forms. This gradient microstructure is consistent with the gradual hardness change from the SZ to the surrounding regions observed in Fig.  7 . Fig. 6 Cross-sectional OM observations of ( a ) measurement locations, ( b ) weld metal, ( c ) HAZ, ( d ) base metal, ( e ) SZ, and ( f ) SZ-HAZ Fig. 7 OM images near the weld toe of the joints and hardness measurement results: ( a ) hardness measurement locations of AW and FSP; ( b ) Vickers hardness variation with distance from the SZ measured along a red line

The microstructural refinement and modification in the SZ significantly improved local mechanical properties, as quantitatively demonstrated by hardness measurements. Figure  7  compares the Vickers hardness distributions at a consistent depth of 1 mm below the surface across both AW and TFSP-treated specimens. The hardness profile clearly reveals distinct hardness gradients corresponding to the microstructural differences described earlier. In the AW specimen, typical hardness values for the base metal, HAZ, and weld metal were approximately 167 Hv, 204 Hv, and 217 Hv, respectively. In comparison, the SZ region in the TFSP-treated specimen displayed dramatically enhanced hardness, with an average peak value reaching approximately 336 Hv—representing an increase of about 54.8% compared to untreated areas. This substantial hardness increment is primarily attributed to TFSP-induced grain refinement and the increased dislocation density associated with severe plastic deformation in the SZ.

Additionally, the hardness profile delineates a gradual transition from the SZ to the SZ-HAZ transition region and the surrounding HAZ, further supporting the gradient microstructure observed in Fig.  6 . The improved hardness in the SZ contributes directly to increased fatigue resistance by enhancing local strength and delaying crack initiation at the critical weld toe regions.

sections.heading: Influence of TFSP on residual stress distribution
paragraphs: Figure  8  shows measured transverse (perpendicular to the weld direction) and longitudinal (parallel to the weld direction) residual stress distributions across both as-welded (AW) and TFSP-treated specimens. Measurement points were systematically positioned at intervals of 5 mm from 15 to 40 mm away from the weld centerline, providing comprehensive insight into residual stress modifications resulting from TFSP. As shown in Fig.  8 (b), transverse residual stresses, which are critical for fatigue crack initiation and propagation at the weld toe, exhibited minimal changes after TFSP treatment compared to the AW condition. Both conditions presented moderate tensile transverse residual stresses across the measurement regions, indicating that the TFSP process did not significantly alter the transverse stress state. The slight increase observed after TFSP can be attributed to localized transverse plastic flow induced by tool rotation. However, because the processed zone is strongly constrained by the surrounding base material, stress relaxation is restricted, and the magnitude of transverse stress modification remains limited. Moreover, notable changes were observed in the longitudinal residual stress distributions (Fig.  8 (c)). Specifically, TFSP introduced higher tensile residual stresses along the longitudinal direction, with measured values distinctly greater than those observed in the AW specimens. This increase is primarily associated with the additional thermomechanical cycle introduced by TFSP. During processing, intense frictional heating and severe plastic deformation occur beneath the rotating tool. Although material softening occurs at elevated temperature, subsequent cooling under significant mechanical constraint from the surrounding rigid material produces non-uniform thermal contraction. The restricted longitudinal shrinkage along the tool travel direction generates additional tensile residual stresses. Because material flow and cumulative plastic strain are predominantly aligned with the processing direction, the longitudinal stress component is more strongly affected than the transverse component. Fig. 8 Residual stress variation with distance from the weld center measured at measuring points: ( a ) surface images of the specimen with residual stress measuring points; ( b ) transverse residual stress; ( c ) longitudinal residual stress

Although TFSP increased the longitudinal residual stress level, transverse residual stress remains the dominant component governing fatigue performance under bending. In bending-dominated loading, the maximum tensile stress develops at the surface and is primarily oriented transverse to the weld toe. Therefore, transverse residual stresses directly superimpose onto the applied tensile stress, increasing the local maximum principal stress and crack-driving force. In contrast, longitudinal residual stresses are not collinear with the principal tensile stress under bending and thus exert comparatively limited influence on crack initiation. Consistent with this stress interaction mechanism, the increase in longitudinal residual stress did not result in measurable deterioration of fatigue life.

Overall, these residual stress measurement results indicate that the primary fatigue life improvements attributed to TFSP arise mainly from geometric smoothing, microstructural refinement, and associated hardness increases at the weld toe, rather than substantial beneficial alterations in transverse residual stresses. This observation underscores the importance of geometry and local mechanical property improvements in enhancing fatigue resistance through TFSP.

sections.heading: Fatigue life improvement by TFSP
Conclusions
paragraphs: Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of TFSP as a practical and highly effective fatigue life enhancement technique for fillet-welded T-joints in steel structures. Future research should focus on further optimization of TFSP parameters, development of robust processing guidelines, and investigation of TFSP’s applicability in fatigue crack repair scenarios to extend structural life and integrity.
